Serving under pressure in recorded men's tennis matches

serve_pressure.Rd

Service points played and won by each player in professional men's matches charted by the Match Charting Project, split into break points, deuce points and all service points. Use it to compare how often a player wins their service points under pressure versus normally.

Usage

serve_pressure

Format

A tibble with 14570 rows and 14 columns. Each row is one player in one match, counting only points where that player was serving.

match_id

Match identifier from the Match Charting Project.

date

Date of the match.

year

Year of the match.

tournament

Tournament name, e.g. "Australian Open".

round

Round of the tournament, e.g. "QF" (quarter-final), "F" (final).

surface

Court surface: "Hard", "Clay" or "Grass".

player

The serving player.

opponent

The player returning serve.

bp_pts

Break points faced: points where losing would lose the service game (e.g. 30-40).

bp_won

Break points won (saved) by the server.

deuce_pts

Points served at deuce (40-40).

deuce_won

Deuce points won by the server.

serve_pts

All points served in the match.

serve_won

All service points won (first- plus second-serve points won).

Source

Match Charting Project by Jeff Sackmann (https://github.com/JeffSackmann/tennis_MatchChartingProject). Licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/).

Details

Break points and deuce points come from the KeyPointsServe file; total service points come from the Overview file.

Cleaning steps (see data-raw/serve_pressure.R):

  • Exact duplicate rows were removed.

  • Matches charted twice with conflicting counts were dropped, because the correct version cannot be identified.

  • Two Davis Cup rows (2024-09-15) with values shifted into the wrong columns were dropped from the match details, removing one match.

  • Matches before 1990 were removed because too few were recorded per year to compare players reliably.

Matches are charted by volunteers, so not all data is recorded. Well-known players and big matches are recorded more often than lesser-known/ lower ranked players. It should be taken as a random sample sample of professional tennis.
